on_screen_labels: Confusion if price and message clash

visual_beats.directive: Four tiles lock into a frame
Clashing price and message flash red
Consistent frame turns green

scenes.voiceover_script: Marketing strategy means the four Ps fit together. A refill product, a fair price, local shop distribution and honest promotion form a connected set. The tiles snap into a single frame around the chosen segment. If the price is high while the message says budget, shoppers feel confused. If promotion promises green benefits but packaging wastes plastic, trust falls. Coherence turns a plan into a position. Because each element reinforces the others, therefore the brand sounds consistent, so customers remember it.

visual_beats.directive: Destination country lights on the map
Revenue bar grows by 600k
Risk meter splits across two markets

scenes.voiceover_script: Entering overseas markets can increase sales and spread risk. Clearleaf Cleaning earns two million dollars at home; a new country adds six hundred thousand, lifting revenue thirty percent and cutting dependence on one market to about seventy seven percent. The map lights up. But cultural differences, lack of knowledge and legal requirements raise difficulty. Customers abroad may prefer bottles, not sachets. Local rules may demand different labels. The gains are real, and so are the costs of learning a new market.

visual_beats.directive: Tariff coin drops onto the ten dollar cart
Landed cost counter reaches twelve
Quota counter stops the next cart

scenes.voiceover_script: Cross border trade can face restrictions. A tariff is a tax on imports: a ten dollar refill gains a two dollar charge, so the landed cost becomes twelve dollars. A quota is a limit on the physical quantity of a product that can be imported, shown by a gate counter that stops at a fixed number. Rules and standards can demand extra tests. These controls protect local producers but raise prices and reduce choice. A firm must price the extra cost into its plan before it enters.

on_screen_labels: Laws protect from faulty and unsafe goods
Pricing and labelling must be clear

visual_beats.directive: Claim shield strikes through an unproven phrase
Price shield adds compulsory charges
Label shield lists ingredients and origin

scenes.voiceover_script: Legal controls on marketing are laws passed by government to protect consumers from faulty goods, unsafe goods and misleading promotion. Three shields rise. Misleading promotion: a claim of completely safe needs evidence, or it is struck through. Pricing: the shown price must include compulsory charges, so there is no surprise at the till. Labelling: ingredients, origin and instructions must be clear. Consumer protection also covers complaints, safety and returns. Clearleaf rewrites its pack claims before shipping, and the shield stays intact.

on_screen_labels: Benefit: returns fall from 5 to 2 percent
Rules build trust and deter rivals

visual_beats.directive: Cost coin drops and scale tilts
Returns bar falls from 5 percent to 2 percent, a drop of 3 percentage points
Trust shield rises and scale settles

scenes.voiceover_script: Regulation has two edges. Compliance costs Clearleaf Cleaning thirty thousand dollars and six weeks of checks, which slows a campaign. Yet clear rules build trust, cut returns from five percent to two percent, and protect reputable firms from unfair rivals. The scales balance a cost coin against a trust shield. Because rules stop rivals making false claims, therefore honest brands look stronger, so customers buy with confidence. A short term expense becomes long term protection.

on_screen_labels: One message: low cost, consistent brand
Adapted: fits local habits and rules
Adapt labels and price, standardise core

visual_beats.directive: Global column stacks cost savings
Local column stacks relevance gains
Verdict banner highlights the blended plan

scenes.voiceover_script: Last decision: standardised or adapted marketing? One global product and message keeps costs low and the brand consistent. Adapting language, pack size and price fits local habits, but every change adds cost and complexity. On the split screen, the left column counts savings; the right column counts relevance. Because refills depend on local words and rules, therefore Clearleaf adapts labels and price, so it standardises the core product only. A smart strategy blends both sides instead of choosing blindly.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Clearleaf Cleaning enters a country where shoppers read local labels and rules require local wording. Which approach fits best?
options: Change the logo and nothing else
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: A split screen shows one global message on the left and local label tiles on the right, then a verdict banner locks onto the blended plan.

videos.video_title: Visualising Productivity, Lean Production and Methods
learning_objectives: Calculate labour productivity and interpret the result.
Compare labour-intensive and capital-intensive production.
Explain lean production, the seven wastes and production methods.

visual_beats.directive: Workshop opens with an empty frame rack
Frames stack rapidly on the rack as the counter rolls to 1,200
Twenty worker icons line up and the owner raises a question mark
A productivity meter rises above the line and holds

scenes.voiceover_script: At Riverbend Bicycle Frames, welders finish 1,200 bicycle frames this month. Twenty production workers made them all. The owner wants one answer: is each worker producing more than last month? Watch frames stack on the rack, workers fade into the background, and a productivity meter rise above the factory floor. That question drives everything in this video.

on_screen_labels: Total output / number of workers (or worker-hours)

elements.text: Labour productivity = total output / number of workers (or worker-hours)
elements.label: 0264 definition

visual_beats.directive: Definition panel slides in from the left
1,200 frames pour through a funnel into the numerator box
Twenty worker icons fill the denominator box and a division bar appears
Result tile flips to 60 frames per worker

scenes.voiceover_script: Labour productivity means output divided by labour input. At Riverbend, total output is 1,200 frames and labour input is 20 workers. Divide 1,200 by 20 and the answer is 60 frames per worker. The counter shows 1,200 frames pouring into one side and 20 worker icons lining the other, then sixty frames sliding into a single worker's column. Because output rose while the workforce stayed the same, unit labour cost falls.

visual_beats.directive: Two blank ratio panels appear side by side
Worker tiles multiply on the labour-intensive side
Machine arms multiply on the capital-intensive side
Both ratio labels settle and a comparison brace appears

scenes.voiceover_script: Now compare two ways to organise work. In the labour-intensive workshop, 20 workers share 2 machines, a ratio of 10 workers per machine. In the capital-intensive line, 8 workers operate 16 machines, so the ratio is 1 worker per 2 machines. Watch the icons slide: worker tiles multiply on the left, machine arms multiply on the right. Capital intensity can lift output per worker, but each machine must be paid for.

on_screen_labels: Just in time: stock is delivered when needed

visual_beats.directive: Tall stacks of tubing fill the left side of the frame
Delivery van pulls in exactly as the line calls for parts
Stock piles melt away and the storage rack empties
Green kaizen loop turns around the workstation

scenes.voiceover_script: Lean production aims to use fewer inputs and cut waste of materials, time and human effort. Riverbend orders tubing just in time, so stock is delivered when needed and storage space shrinks. Kaizen means continuous improvement through eliminating waste, with worker suggestions adjusting the jig each week. Watch stock piles melt, a delivery van sync with the line, and improvement loops turn. Therefore fewer resources are tied up, so unit costs fall.

scenes.on_screen_title: The Seven Wastes of Lean Production
on_screen_labels: Seven wastes flash red, then turn green

visual_beats.directive: Seven grey waste icons appear in a row
Each icon flashes red as its waste is named
A green fix badge replaces each red icon in turn
The whole row turns green and a value stream strip lights up

scenes.voiceover_script: Lean thinking names seven wastes. Overproduction stacks unsold frames; waiting leaves welders idle; transport drags parts across the floor; over-processing polishes hidden joints; inventory piles up; motion means reaching and walking; defects send frames back for rework. Each icon flashes red, then a green lean fix replaces it. Because every waste adds cost without adding value, removing one waste at a time raises productivity.

on_screen_labels: Batch: ten red, then ten blue

visual_beats.directive: Three empty assembly lines fade in side by side
One custom frame moves alone on the job line
Ten red then ten blue frames move on the batch line
A continuous stream of frames flows on the third line

scenes.voiceover_script: Three production methods suit three orders. Job production makes one bespoke item: a custom frame is measured, cut and welded alone. Batch production makes a quantity of one design, then switches to another: ten red frames, then ten blue. Flow production runs large volumes continuously: frames move down an automated line without stopping. Watch three assembly lines appear side by side, with a single unique frame, labelled groups, and a steady stream. Because volume and variety differ, the right method changes.

visual_beats.directive: A frame drawing rotates in three dimensions on a CAD screen
The drawing compresses into a digital file and flies right
A CAM machine receives the file and cuts a tube
A robot arm welds the frame with no worker hands

scenes.voiceover_script: Technology changes how the frame is made. Computer-aided design, or CAD, lets engineers draw and modify the frame on screen. Computer-aided manufacturing, or CAM, sends that design to computer-controlled machines that cut and weld it. Automation keeps the line running with minimal human control. Watch the design rotate in three dimensions, travel as a digital file, and become a real frame. Output becomes more consistent, though software failures can stop everything.

scenes.on_screen_title: Lean and Technology: Help or Hindrance?
on_screen_labels: Judgement depends on reliability and skills

visual_beats.directive: A vertical line splits the screen into two panels
Green markers show waste and unit cost falling
Amber icons show a late van and a training invoice
A balance scale tips toward a conditional judgement

scenes.voiceover_script: Does lean production and technology always help? On one side, Riverbend cuts waste, raises output per worker and lowers unit costs. On the other side, just in time leaves no buffer if a supplier is late, and automation needs costly training. Watch a split screen: green cost markers fall on the left, risk icons flash on the right. Benefit: lower costs. Risk: supply delays and retraining.
syllabus_concepts_tagged: advantages and disadvantages of lean production

visual_beats.directive: A taller stack of 1,440 frames slides in
The stack divides into twenty equal columns
Each column fills to 72 frames
The old 60-frame marker fades and the 72 tile glows

scenes.voiceover_script: Time to apply the idea. If Riverbend raises output to 1,440 frames with the same 20 workers, what is the labour productivity? Choose the calculation: divide 1,440 by 20, not by 2. The answer is 72 frames per worker, up from 60. Watch the counter divide the stack into twenty columns, then compare the new tile with the old marker to see the gain.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Riverbend makes 1,440 frames with 20 workers. What is labour productivity per worker?
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: An animated stack of 1,440 frames splits into 20 equal worker columns; each column fills to 72 frames while a red 60-frame marker slides away.

videos.chapter_title: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
videos.video_title: Visualising Break-Even Charts & Margin of Safety
learning_objectives: Classify fixed, variable and total costs.
Explain economies and diseconomies of scale.
Construct and interpret a break-even chart and margin of safety.
Evaluate the limitations of break-even analysis.

visual_beats.directive: Bakery counter opens empty with ovens in the background
Coins stack up to 2,000 dollars for rent
A variable-cost pipe begins to fill with each loaf
A ghost break-even chart fades in at the right

scenes.voiceover_script: At Stonehaven Bakehouse, ovens cost 2,000 dollars a month whether they bake one loaf or one thousand. Each loaf uses two dollars of flour and energy. The manager asks: how many loaves must we sell before the bakery stops losing money? Watch coins fill a fixed-cost stack, a variable-cost pipe grow with every loaf, and a break-even line appear.

scenes.on_screen_title: Fixed, Variable and Total Cost Pipes

visual_beats.directive: Fixed pipe holds a constant 2,000 dollar level
Loaves drop into the variable pipe and it rises by 2 dollars each
At 1,000 loaves the variable pipe reads 2,000 dollars
Both pipes merge and the total counter lands on 4,000 dollars

scenes.voiceover_script: Fixed costs do not vary in the short run with output: rent stays 2,000 dollars. Variable costs rise directly with output: two dollars for every loaf. At 1,000 loaves, variable cost is 1,000 times 2, which equals 2,000 dollars. Total cost is fixed plus variable, so 2,000 plus 2,000 gives 4,000 dollars. Watch the blue pipe hold steady, the orange pipe climb, and the total counter reach 4,000.

on_screen_labels: Long-run average cost falls, then rises

visual_beats.directive: Axes appear with output on the horizontal axis
Three descending points pulse as average cost falls to 4 dollars and 50 cents
The curve bottoms out and a technical economy label appears
The fourth point pulses at 5 dollars and 50 cents as communication problems appear

scenes.voiceover_script: Long-run average cost often falls, then rises. For a larger bakery, 400 loaves cost 3,200 dollars, so average is 8 dollars. At 800 loaves, total cost is 4,000 dollars, giving 5 dollars average. At 1,200 loaves it is 5,400 dollars, so 4 dollars and 50 cents. But at 1,600 loaves, total cost reaches 8,800 dollars, pushing average back to 5 dollars and 50 cents. Watch the U-curve dip and climb.

on_screen_labels: Break-even: total revenue equals total cost

elements.text: Break-even output = fixed costs / (selling price - variable cost per unit)
elements.label: 0264 definition

visual_beats.directive: The break-even formula drops into the centre
Price 6 and variable cost 2 slide into the brackets
The contribution tile flips to 4 dollars per loaf
2,000 divided by 4 lands on a marker at 500 loaves

scenes.voiceover_script: Break-even output is fixed costs divided by price minus variable cost per unit. At Stonehaven, price is 6 dollars and variable cost is 2 dollars, so contribution is 4 dollars per loaf. Divide fixed costs of 2,000 by 4 and the answer is 500 loaves. Watch the formula appear, the numbers drop into place, and a glowing marker stop at 500 on the output axis. At that point profit is zero.

visual_beats.directive: Horizontal and vertical axes grow from the origin with tick labels
The blue fixed-cost line draws flat at 2,000 dollars
Orange total cost reaches 4,000 and green revenue reaches 6,000 at 1,000 loaves
The crossing pulses red with a label of 500 loaves and 3,000 dollars

scenes.voiceover_script: Now build the full break-even chart. The horizontal axis shows output from zero to 1,000 loaves; the vertical axis shows dollars from zero to 6,000. A blue fixed-cost line sits flat at 2,000. An orange total-cost line starts at 2,000 and climbs by 2 dollars per loaf, reaching 4,000 at 1,000 loaves. A green revenue line starts at zero and climbs by 6 dollars per loaf, reaching 6,000. They cross exactly at 500 loaves and 3,000 dollars. Watch each line draw itself, then the crossing point pulse red.

visual_beats.directive: A vertical guide rises at 1,000 loaves
Orange and green markers meet the guide at 4,000 and 6,000
The distance between them fills with a green band
A 2,000 dollar profit tile pops out of the band

scenes.voiceover_script: Read the chart at 1,000 loaves. Total cost is 2,000 fixed plus 2,000 variable, giving 4,000 dollars. Total revenue is 1,000 times 6, giving 6,000 dollars. Revenue exceeds cost by 2,000 dollars, so the bakery makes a 2,000 dollar profit. Above 500 loaves it earns a profit; below 500 it makes a loss. Watch a vertical guide rise at 1,000, and a green profit bar grow between the two lines.

on_screen_labels: Margin of safety = actual output - break-even output

visual_beats.directive: A marker appears at 700 loaves on the output axis
The 500 marker glows and a band stretches between them
Revenue 4,200 and cost 3,400 appear as paired tiles
An 800 dollar profit tile settles above the band

scenes.voiceover_script: Margin of safety is actual output minus break-even output. Stonehaven expects to sell 700 loaves, so 700 minus 500 equals 200 loaves of safety. Sales could fall by 200 loaves before a loss appears. At 700 loaves, revenue is 4,200 dollars and total cost is 3,400 dollars, leaving 800 dollars profit. Watch the 700 marker move left toward 500, with a 200-loaf safety band shrinking between them.

scenes.on_screen_title: How Far Can Break-Even Be Trusted?
on_screen_labels: One product and known demand assumed

visual_beats.directive: A clean break-even chart sits in the left panel
A green planning tick appears beside the crossing
Amber question marks multiply over prices, costs and demand in the right panel
A caption fades in: a planning aid, not a guarantee

scenes.voiceover_script: Is break-even useful? It shows the output needed to avoid a loss and the cushion above it. Yet it assumes constant prices and costs, one product, and known demand, while real bakeries sell many lines with uncertain sales. Watch a split screen: green planning gains on the left, amber question marks over fixed assumptions on the right. Because the model simplifies reality, it guides decisions but never guarantees profit.

visual_beats.directive: The fixed line jumps from 2,000 to 2,400 dollars
Contribution stays at 4 dollars per loaf
The crossing slides right from 500 to 600 loaves
A 600-loaf tile glows as the old marker fades

scenes.voiceover_script: If fixed costs rise to 2,400 dollars and price stays 6 dollars with variable cost 2 dollars, what is the new break-even output? Contribution remains 4 dollars, so divide 2,400 by 4. The answer is 600 loaves. Watch the fixed-cost line jump up and the crossing slide from 500 to 600.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Fixed costs rise to $2,400 while price stays $6 and variable cost stays $2. What is the new break-even output?
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: The blue fixed-cost line jumps from 2,000 to 2,400 dollars; the revenue and total-cost lines now cross at a pulsing marker labelled 600 loaves, with the old 500 marker fading.

videos.video_title: Visualising Quality Control, Assurance and Failure Costs
learning_objectives: Distinguish quality control from quality assurance.
Explain total quality management, kaizen, quality circles and benchmarking.
Calculate defect rates and costs of failure.
Evaluate the costs and benefits of achieving quality.

visual_beats.directive: Good assemblies move along a conveyor toward packing
Red defective units drop through the inspection gate
A reject bin fills and a cost meter starts ticking
A manager silhouette asks whether end checks are enough

scenes.voiceover_script: At Northgate Medical Devices, a final inspection gate holds back faulty syringe assemblies. Workers check 2,000 units each week, and about 5 percent fail. Each failure costs 12 dollars to rework. The manager wonders whether checking at the end is enough. Watch red defective units drop out at the gate while good units move to packing, and a cost meter tick upward.

on_screen_labels: Quality control: check at end of process
Quality assurance: standards checked at each stage

visual_beats.directive: Left panel shows one inspection gate at the end of the line
Red units are rejected after all the work is finished
Right panel shows green check loops at every workstation
Stage labels light up from components through to packing

scenes.voiceover_script: Quality control means checking for quality at the end of the production process. At Northgate the inspection gate rejects bad assemblies, but the waste has already happened. Quality assurance means setting quality standards throughout the process and checking they are reached at each stage. Watch a split screen: on the left, one gate catches defects; on the right, a loop of checks wraps every stage, from components to packing.

on_screen_labels: Quality circles solve defects at source

visual_beats.directive: Small green loop indicators spin at three workstations
A circle of worker icons forms around a defect card
The loops merge into one large TQM loop around the factory
Fewer red units travel toward the final gate

scenes.voiceover_script: Total quality management makes quality everyone's responsibility. Kaizen means continuous improvement through eliminating waste, so Northgate's teams tweak the assembly jig every week. Quality circles bring workers together to solve defects at their source. Watch small green loop indicators spin at each workstation, then merge into one large TQM loop encircling the whole factory. Because problems are caught early, fewer faulty units reach the gate.

visual_beats.directive: A grey bar grows to 5 percent and holds
A green benchmark line draws at 1 percent
The space between them shades amber
A target pointer moves from the bar toward the line

scenes.voiceover_script: Benchmarking compares Northgate's performance with the best in the industry. The best assembler has a 1 percent defect rate, while Northgate starts at 5 percent. That gap sets a target rather than a guess. Watch two bars race upward: a grey 5 percent bar for Northgate and a green 1 percent benchmark line, with the gap shaded.

visual_beats.directive: A counter rolls to 2,000 assemblies
A red slice detaches and reads 100 defective units
Red units slide into the rework bin one by one
A 1,200 dollar cost tile flips up beside the bin

scenes.voiceover_script: Let's calculate the cost of failure before improvement. Northgate makes 2,000 assemblies a week and 5 percent are defective. Multiply 2,000 by 5 percent, which is 2,000 times 0.05, giving 100 defective units. Each one costs 12 dollars to rework. Multiply 100 by 12 and the weekly rework bill is 1,200 dollars. Watch the output counter split, 100 red units slide into a rework bin, and a 1,200 dollar cost tile appear.

scenes.on_screen_title: Cost of Failure After Quality Assurance

visual_beats.directive: The red slice shrinks from 100 to 40 units
The rework cost tile flips from 1,200 to 480 dollars
A saving counter climbs to 720 dollars a week
Fifty week icons march past and the total reaches 36,000 dollars

scenes.voiceover_script: After quality assurance and kaizen at Northgate, the defect rate falls to just 2 percent. Now 2,000 times 0.02 gives 40 defective units. At 12 dollars each, rework costs 480 dollars a week. That is 1,200 minus 480, a saving of 720 dollars every week. Across 50 working weeks, 720 times 50 equals 36,000 dollars saved. Watch the red bin shrink from 100 to 40 units while the saving counter climbs to 36,000.

visual_beats.directive: Defects enter the top of a funnel
Two streams split into internal red and external amber
Return boxes and goodwill icons appear on the amber stream
A green shield at the top blocks units before defects form

scenes.voiceover_script: Failure cost is not just rework. Internal failure covers scrap and rework before delivery. External failure covers returns, guarantee claims and lost goodwill after delivery. Prevention and appraisal costs are spent to stop those failures happening. Watch a funnel: defects divide into an internal red stream and an external amber stream, while a green prevention shield blocks units upstream.

visual_beats.directive: A split screen opens with two empty panels
Green bars rise as rework and returns fall
Amber training invoices and clock icons stack on the right
A balance line settles on a two-sided conclusion

scenes.voiceover_script: Does chasing zero defects pay? For Northgate, quality assurance cuts rework, returns and reputation damage, and the weekly saving is clear. Against it, training, new equipment and quality circles cost time and money, and inspection at every stage can slow output. Watch a split screen: green saving bars rise on the left, amber cost and delay icons stack on the right. So the benefit is fewer failures, but the cost is real.
syllabus_concepts_tagged: advantages and disadvantages of quality assurance

visual_beats.directive: The output counter doubles from 2,000 to 4,000
The red defect slice grows wider
The x 0.02 multiplier glows between the output tile and the result tile
A tile flips from 40 to 80 defective units

scenes.voiceover_script: Apply it. If Northgate's output rises to 4,000 units a week and the 2 percent defect rate holds, how many units are defective? Multiply 4,000 by 0.02 to get 80. Watch the counter duplicate the line, then 80 red units drop into the bin instead of 40.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Northgate raises weekly output to 4,000 units while the defect rate stays at 2 percent. How many units are defective?
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: The output counter doubles from 2,000 to 4,000, the red defect slice grows, and a tile flips from 40 to 80 defective units as 0.02 appears.

videos.video_title: Visualising Location Decisions with Cost Comparisons
learning_objectives: Distinguish quantitative from qualitative location factors.
Compare site costs using a worked numerical example.
Explain how changing demand can shift the best location.
Evaluate a location decision using both numbers and judgement.

on_screen_labels: Manufacturers weigh labour, transport, raw materials, power, land and government incentives

elements.label: Six location factors including government incentives

visual_beats.directive: A regional map fades in with a river and a coastline
Two pins drop onto the port and the capital
Six factor icons, including government incentives, orbit each pin
A plant silhouette appears at each site in turn

scenes.voiceover_script: Frostvale Foods is choosing a site for a new frozen-food plant. Two pins glow on the map: one near the port, one near the capital city. The finance team must decide where to build. Watch the map zoom, the two pins pulse, and six factor icons, including government incentives, orbit each location. The decision will mix hard numbers with softer judgements.

visual_beats.directive: A blank cost column grows beside the port pin
Labour and transport tiles drop in with their values
Materials, utilities and the green incentive tile follow
The counter starts adding the five tiles

scenes.voiceover_script: Quantitative factors can be measured in money. Labour costs, transport to market, raw material delivery, utilities and government incentives all have price tags. At the port site, labour is 300,000 dollars, transport 80,000, materials 40,000 and utilities 60,000, with a 30,000 dollar incentive. Watch each cost label drop into a column and a total counter begin adding them up before any decision is made.

on_screen_labels: Quality of life attracts skilled staff

visual_beats.directive: The cost column stays visible on the left
A lifestyle panel fades in with homes and schools
A skills badge and a clean river panel appear
A bracket joins the three panels to the decision

scenes.voiceover_script: Qualitative factors are harder to price. Quality of life affects whether skilled engineers want to move. Local labour skills affect training time. Environmental impact affects the plant's reputation and licence to operate. Watch three translucent panels fade in beside the cost column: a lifestyle icon, a skills badge and a green river. These factors cannot be ignored simply because they lack a price tag.

scenes.on_screen_title: Total Annual Cost at Site A

visual_beats.directive: Labour and transport tiles stack to 380,000 dollars
Materials and utilities push the counter to 480,000
The green incentive tile flips sign and slides in
The total settles on 450,000 dollars a year

scenes.voiceover_script: Let's total the port site, called Site A, using annual costs. Labour 300,000 dollars plus transport 80,000 gives 380,000. Add raw material delivery of 40,000 to reach 420,000. Add utilities of 60,000 to reach 480,000. Now subtract the government incentive of 30,000, leaving 450,000 dollars a year. Watch five cost tiles stack in the column, with the green incentive tile flipping the total down to 450,000. That is the number to beat.

scenes.on_screen_title: Total Annual Cost at Site B

visual_beats.directive: Four cost tiles stack beside the capital pin
The counter steps through 380,000 and 450,000 to 500,000
A second bar rises beside the first column
A 50,000 dollar saving badge appears on Site A

scenes.voiceover_script: Now let us total the city site, called Site B, carefully. Labour 360,000, transport 20,000, materials 70,000 and utilities 50,000, with no incentive. Add them: 360,000 plus 20,000 is 380,000; plus 70,000 is 450,000; plus 50,000 gives 500,000 dollars. Site A is 50,000 dollars cheaper. Watch the second column rise to 500,000, with a 50,000 dollar saving badge on Site A based on today's demand.

visual_beats.directive: The transport tile grows from 80,000 to 140,000 dollars
The increase badge reads 60,000 dollars
Site A total rolls from 450,000 to 510,000
Site B total stays at 500,000 and takes the winning glow

scenes.voiceover_script: Now demand shifts toward the capital city. Serving that market from the port becomes costlier: Site A's transport rises from 80,000 to 140,000 dollars, an increase of 60,000. Recalculate Site A: 300,000 plus 140,000 plus 40,000 plus 60,000 minus 30,000 equals 510,000 dollars. Site B stays at 500,000, so it is now 10,000 dollars cheaper. Watch the transport tile grow and the totals swap places as customers move closer to the city.

scenes.on_screen_title: The Chosen Pin Moves With Demand

visual_beats.directive: Demand dots cluster densely around the capital
The port pin dims and the city pin brightens
A truck retraces a longer route from the port
The chosen pin slides across the map to the city

scenes.voiceover_script: The map tells the same story. As buyers cluster in the capital, the port pin dims and the city pin brightens. Because transport cost rises with distance, the landed cost of frozen meals rises; therefore the cheaper site changes; so Frostvale should shift its plant toward the city. Watch a delivery truck retrace a longer route, then the chosen pin slide across the map.

scenes.on_screen_title: Numbers Guide, But Do Not Settle
on_screen_labels: Port may offer cheaper land and skills
Quality of life and environment matter

visual_beats.directive: A green bar shows the 10,000 dollar annual saving
Amber panels fade in with land, skills and wage icons
A river and lifestyle icon join the right panel
A judgement scale settles between the two sides

scenes.voiceover_script: Should Frostvale choose purely on cost? After the demand shift, the city site saves 10,000 dollars a year. Yet the port may offer skilled workers and cheaper land, while the city brings higher wages and tighter rules. Watch a split screen: a green saving badge on one side, amber quality of life and environment icons on the other. So cost guides the choice, but it does not settle it alone.

scenes.on_screen_title: Apply It: A Bigger Transport Shock

visual_beats.directive: The transport pipe stretches by another 20,000 dollars
The Site A total rolls from 510,000 to 530,000
A red gap bar grows above the 500,000 dollar column
A 30,000 dollar answer tile glows

scenes.voiceover_script: Apply the idea. If Site A's transport rose to 160,000 dollars instead of 140,000, by how much would its total exceed Site B's? Add 20,000 to 510,000 for 530,000. That is 30,000 above 500,000. Watch the transport tile stretch and the cost gap widen on screen.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: With transport at $160,000, Site A's total cost rises to $530,000. How much more is that than Site B's $500,000?
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: Two cost columns animate side by side; the port column climbs from 510,000 to 530,000 dollars while a red gap bar stretches to 30,000 above the city column.

videos.video_title: The Finance Fountain: Needs and Sources
learning_objectives: Distinguish start-up capital from working capital and short-term from long-term needs
Identify internal and external sources of finance with 0264 terms
Evaluate debt against equity using a concrete funding plan

scenes.on_screen_title: Can Finance Fill the Kayak Gap?

visual_beats.directive: Show empty garage with order slips piling up
Fountain basin fills with blue coins
Label finance with the exact textbook wording
Coin stream reaches the workshop door

scenes.voiceover_script: Meet Northwater Kayaks, a small firm making sea kayaks in a converted garage. Demand is rising, but the owner cannot build more boats with cash alone. Finance is money or capital needed to pay for expenditure and business operations. Without it, orders wait, stock runs short and growth stalls. Watch the finance fountain fill the business, one source at a time, right now, before the summer season.

scenes.on_screen_title: Five Reasons a Business Needs Finance

elements.label: Short lane and long lane divider
Need tiles flow into two lanes

visual_beats.directive: Five need tiles slide into view
Stock bills drop into the short lane
Machine and factory tiles drop into the long lane
Lane labels lock in place

scenes.voiceover_script: Businesses need finance for five clear reasons. Start-up capital pays for essential assets before trading begins. Expansion funds new premises and bigger output. Replacing worn non-current assets keeps production running. New technology raises efficiency and lowers unit costs. Working capital pays day-to-day bills. Match the time period to the source: stock and monthly bills are short-term, repaid within one year; machinery and factory expansion are long-term, repaid over many years.

visual_beats.directive: Machine price tag counts to fifty thousand
Stock crate fills with timber and fabric
Total counter locks at sixty-two thousand
Two streams separate with clock badges

scenes.voiceover_script: Here is Northwater's concrete plan. A new moulding machine costs fifty thousand dollars and will last five years. Extra timber and fabric stock costs twelve thousand dollars and sells within three months. The total need is sixty-two thousand dollars. Because one machine is long-term and the stock is short-term, a single source cannot sensibly fund both. So the finance fountain must divide into two separate streams of different lengths.

visual_beats.directive: Three source tiles appear above the funnel
Savings tile drops and counts ten thousand
Retained profit and trailer tiles follow
Reservoir shows twenty-five thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Internal finance comes from within the business or its owners. Three tiles drop into the fountain: ten thousand dollars of the owner's savings, twelve thousand dollars of retained profit, and three thousand dollars from selling an old trailer. That gives twenty-five thousand dollars. Internal finance avoids interest payments and keeps control with the owner. The limit is size: savings are finite, and spending retained profit leaves less cash for emergencies.

elements.label: Government grant and trade credit tiles

visual_beats.directive: Loan tile slides along the long blue pipe
Overdraft tile slides along the short green pipe
Share grant and credit tiles stack at the side
Counter confirms thirty-seven thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: External finance comes from sources outside the business. A five-year bank loan supplies twenty-five thousand dollars for the machine. A twelve-thousand-dollar overdraft covers stock for three months. A share issue, a government grant or trade credit are other external tiles. External sources raise large sums quickly, but loans charge interest and must be repaid whether profit rises or falls. An overdraft suits a temporary gap, never a ten-year factory expansion.

visual_beats.directive: Loan panel lists predictable interest
Repayment clock appears even in a weak sales month
Share panel shows no fixed repayment
Control tiles shift to new investors

scenes.voiceover_script: Compare debt with equity on the split screen. A bank loan keeps ownership with the founder, and interest is predictable. But repayments continue when sales fall, and the machine may be used as security. Issuing shares brings cash with no fixed repayment or interest, and investors share the risk. The cost is dilution: existing owners give up a slice of control and future dividends. Neither source is free; the right choice depends on duration, cost and legal form.

visual_beats.directive: Short bar appears with stock icon
Long bar appears with machine icon
Repayment coins travel back along both bars
Total funding counter locks at sixty-two thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Put the sources on a timeline. In months one to three, the overdraft finances stock and is repaid as kayaks sell. Across years one to five, the bank loan pays for the moulding machine as it earns revenue. Because the stock cycle is short and the machine is long-lived, therefore each source is matched to its purpose, so the business lowers its refinancing risk. The internal twenty-five thousand dollars reduces borrowing, and retained profit stays as a cushion.

elements.label: Sole trader cannot sell public shares

visual_beats.directive: Seven factor chips line up across the top
Pros panel fills with green tiles
Cons panel fills with red tiles
Fountain closes over the balanced decision

scenes.voiceover_script: Before choosing, a finance manager checks seven factors: business size, legal form, amount needed, length of time, existing loans, cost and purpose. A sole trader cannot sell shares to the public, so internal cash or a bank loan is realistic. A larger company can issue equity but gives up control. Advantages sit beside limitations: speed against interest, control against dilution, flexibility against repayment. Finance keeps a kayak business afloat only when the source fits the need.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Northwater needs $12,000 for timber and fabric that will sell within three months. Which source is most suitable?
options: A five-year bank loan secured on the workshop
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: A three-month calendar is placed beside a $12,000 stock crate; the overdraft tile slides in and shrinks as sales coins come back, while the five-year loan tile is crossed out.

videos.video_title: Coin Streams: Cash-Flow Forecasting in Motion
learning_objectives: Complete a cash-flow forecast using net cash flow and closing balance rules
Explain why a profitable business can still run out of cash
Evaluate forecast limitations and short-term remedies

visual_beats.directive: Cafe crowd orders animate in
Till counter drops below the invoice
Invoice stamp flashes red
Coin stream label cash appears

scenes.voiceover_script: Lantern Lane City Cafes serves thousands of lunches, yet the owner cannot pay the milk supplier this Friday. Profit is revenue minus costs over a period; cash is money available now. A cash-flow forecast is an estimate of future cash inflows and outflows, usually month by month, showing the expected closing balance. A profitable business can still run out of cash when customers pay later and suppliers demand payment now. Follow the coin streams to find the gap.

elements.label: Cash inflows row with blue coins
Cash outflows row with orange coins

visual_beats.directive: Table rows draw themselves one by one
Blue coins enter the inflow row
Orange coins leave the outflow row
Balance row glows with the rule

scenes.voiceover_script: A cash-flow forecast has five features. Cash inflows are sums received, such as cafe takings. Cash outflows are sums paid, such as wages, rent and ingredients. Net cash flow is the difference between inflows and outflows during each period. Opening balance is cash at the start; closing balance is cash at the end. The rule is simple: closing balance equals opening balance plus net cash flow. Every row becomes a moving coin stream.

elements.label: Balance bar sixteen thousand then eleven thousand

visual_beats.directive: Opening balance eight thousand appears
Net flow plus eight thousand fills the bar
Month two outflow stream overtakes inflow
Bar settles at eleven thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Build the forecast with Lantern Lane. Month one opens with eight thousand dollars. Inflows are thirty thousand; outflows are twenty-two thousand, so net cash flow is plus eight thousand and closing balance is sixteen thousand. Month two receives twenty-six thousand and pays thirty-one thousand, giving net cash flow of minus five thousand. Sixteen thousand plus negative five thousand leaves eleven thousand. Blue coins flow in, orange coins flow out, and the balance bar rises then dips.

elements.label: Month three and four inflow coins
Four net flows summed to minus twelve thousand

visual_beats.directive: Month three row highlights the ten thousand gap
Closing bar nearly reaches zero
Month four net flow turns the bar red
Axis shows negative four thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Month three opens at eleven thousand. Inflows fall to twenty-four thousand, outflows climb to thirty-four thousand, so net cash flow is minus ten thousand and closing balance is one thousand. Month four opens at one thousand, receives twenty-eight thousand, pays thirty-three thousand, and ends four thousand dollars in the red. Add the four net flows: plus eight, minus five, minus ten, minus five equals minus twelve thousand. Eight thousand opening cash minus twelve thousand gives negative four thousand.

visual_beats.directive: Profit column builds from sales
Invoice tile floats but becomes no coin
Stock bags pile up in the middle
Cash column drains as bills land

scenes.voiceover_script: Why can a profitable cafe chain still have no cash? Because credit sales become trade receivables, not coins. Because extra coffee beans sit as inventory before they are sold. And because suppliers, wages and rent must be paid immediately. Profit measures performance over a period; cash measures survival this week. Therefore a growing business can report a healthy profit while its bank balance empties, so the forecast must track timing, not just totals.

visual_beats.directive: Cash coin enters the inventory node
Inventory moves into production
Receivable invoice turns into a coin
Working capital card shows five thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: The working capital cycle shows the same trap. Cash buys inventory; inventory moves into production and service delivery; sales create receivables; then customers finally pay and cash returns. Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, the finance needed for day-to-day expenses. Lantern Lane holds twenty thousand dollars of current assets and fifteen thousand of current liabilities, so working capital is five thousand dollars. Too little working capital risks insolvency; too much sits idle.

visual_beats.directive: Negative four thousand bar appears
Overdraft tile lifts bar to plus one thousand
Supplier relationship tile wobbles
Customer goodwill tile dips slightly

scenes.voiceover_script: A negative closing balance signals a shortfall, so Lantern Lane needs a five-thousand-dollar overdraft. That facility covers the four-thousand-dollar gap and leaves one thousand dollars of headroom. Delaying supplier payments or asking customers to pay sooner also helps. An overdraft is flexible and quick, but interest charges grow if the gap lasts. Late payments strain supplier relationships and can stop deliveries. Asking customers to pay faster improves cash, yet may cost goodwill.

scenes.on_screen_title: What a Forecast Cannot Tell You

elements.label: Cold spell and broken oven surprises

visual_beats.directive: Estimate badges pop up on each cell
Surprise icons break two flow links
Warning light turns green before the gap
Split panel holds the judgement

scenes.voiceover_script: Forecasts have limits. They depend on estimates: a cold spell raises sales, a broken oven adds costs, and customers may pay late. A cash-flow forecast is not a profit forecast and cannot predict surprises. Used with care, it warns of a gap before it becomes a crisis, letting the owner obtain finance in time. Because timing decides survival, a small cafe with steady profit still watches every coin stream.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Lantern Lane expects a closing balance of -$4,000 next month. Which response protects cash without damaging future trade most?
options: Buy a new delivery van now
Obtain a short-term overdraft and chase receivables
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: The balance bar dips below zero, then an overdraft tile lifts it above zero while invoice flows from customers turn into coins; the van and extra-stock tiles grey out.

videos.video_title: The Vertical Income Statement, Row by Row
learning_objectives: Build an Income Statement from revenue through retained profit
Calculate gross profit and profit with a worked numeric example
Evaluate what profit shows and what it hides

visual_beats.directive: Van and installed fences fade in
Blank statement sheet unrolls
First revenue figure drops into place
Empty rows light up in sequence

scenes.voiceover_script: Picketline Fencing Co installs garden fences, but its owner cannot explain where the money went. Sales were busy all year, yet the bank balance barely moved. An Income Statement records income and all costs incurred to earn that income over a period, usually a year. It is built vertically, line by line, from revenue down to retained profit. Watch each figure drop into place like a fence post.

visual_beats.directive: Revenue card locks at the top
Material icons stack into cost of sales
Subtraction line draws downward
Gross profit counter locks at seventy-five thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Start at the top with revenue. Revenue is the income from selling goods or services during a period. Picketline billed one hundred twenty thousand dollars for fencing jobs last year. Cost of sales is the cost of the posts, rails, concrete and gates actually used on those jobs: forty-five thousand dollars. Subtract cost of sales from revenue. One hundred twenty thousand minus forty-five thousand gives gross profit of seventy-five thousand dollars.

elements.label: Fitter wages van fuel insurance and rent

visual_beats.directive: Expense icons line up in a row
Overheads total counts to thirty-eight thousand
Subtraction line sweeps across
Profit counter locks at thirty-seven thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Gross profit is made when revenue is greater than cost of sales. It shows the margin earned before overheads. Now subtract expenses, the fixed costs and overheads of the period. Picketline spent thirty-eight thousand dollars on fitter wages, van fuel, insurance and yard rent. Seventy-five thousand minus thirty-eight thousand leaves profit of thirty-seven thousand dollars. Profit is total income less total costs, and it rewards the owner for risk-taking.

visual_beats.directive: Profit counter reaches the first gate
Tax removes seven thousand
Dividends remove ten thousand
Retained profit reserves twenty thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Profit is not the same as cash in the owner's pocket. First deduct tax of seven thousand dollars. Thirty-seven thousand minus seven thousand leaves thirty thousand dollars. Then pay dividends of ten thousand dollars to the shareholders. Thirty thousand minus ten thousand leaves retained profit of twenty thousand dollars. Retained profit is the earnings kept in the business for growth, perhaps a second van or a wider stock of fencing materials.

visual_beats.directive: Profit tile branches into four outcomes
Retained profit flows to a new van icon
Borrowing tile shrinks as profit grows
Year labels scroll for comparison

scenes.voiceover_script: Why does profit matter? It is a reward for risk-taking and a source of finance for expansion. It measures success and attracts investors and lenders. Because retained profit can fund a new van, therefore the firm borrows less, so future interest costs fall. Comparing this Income Statement with last year's reveals whether material costs or overheads are rising. A falling profit warns the owner before the problem becomes a crisis.

elements.label: Revenue bar one hundred twenty thousand

visual_beats.directive: Revenue bar stretches across the frame
Cost segments peel away from the bar
Profit bar settles at about one third
Two-step formula card flashes

scenes.voiceover_script: Do not confuse revenue with profit. Revenue is the total sales income: one hundred twenty thousand dollars. Profit is what remains after costs: thirty-seven thousand dollars. On screen, the revenue bar stretches across the frame while the profit bar is only a fraction as long. A firm can grow revenue and still see profit shrink if costs rise faster. Always show the calculation in two steps: revenue minus cost of sales, then minus expenses.

on_screen_labels: Misses cash timing and asset value

visual_beats.directive: Left panel lists what profit reveals
Clock icon shows late customer payment
Asset and goodwill tiles stay hidden
Three statements sit side by side

scenes.voiceover_script: Now evaluate what profit does and does not show. It shows whether trading earned more than it cost, and it helps compare years. It does not show cash timing, so a profitable firm can still miss a supplier payment. It does not show the value of assets, the quality of fences or customer goodwill. Historic figures look backward. Use the Income Statement beside a cash-flow forecast and a statement of financial position before deciding.

visual_beats.directive: Top revenue row locks in
Gross profit and profit rows follow
Tax and dividend gates close
Retained profit seals the statement

scenes.voiceover_script: Let us rebuild the whole vertical statement in one pass. Revenue one hundred twenty thousand; cost of sales forty-five thousand; gross profit seventy-five thousand; expenses thirty-eight thousand; profit thirty-seven thousand; tax seven thousand; dividends ten thousand; retained profit twenty thousand. Each row locks into place like a completed panel. The advantage is clarity; the limitation is that one period never tells the whole story of a fencing business. Compare several years before judging performance.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Picketline's revenue rose from $120,000 to $132,000 while cost of sales rose from $45,000 to $56,250. What happened to gross profit?
options: It rose from $75,000 to $75,750, but the gross margin fell
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: Both revenue bars grow; the red cost segment expands faster in percentage terms, the green gross-profit segment grows only from $75,000 to $75,750, and a margin dial turns down from 62.50% to 57.39%.

videos.video_title: Balance Scales: The Statement of Financial Position
learning_objectives: Identify non-current assets, current assets, liabilities and equity
Calculate total assets, working capital and capital employed
Assess liquidity and evaluate the snapshot limitation

on_screen_labels: Liabilities and equity on the right

elements.label: Balance scale frozen on one date

visual_beats.directive: Balance beam appears level
Assets drop onto the left pan
Liabilities and equity drop onto the right pan
Date stamp reads one particular time

scenes.voiceover_script: Paw and Polish Grooming sells shampoos, brushes and grooming sessions. An Income Statement covers a period; a statement of financial position shows the value of assets and liabilities at a particular time. Picture a balance scale frozen on one date. On the left sit assets; on the right sit liabilities and equity. The scale must balance, because everything the business owns was funded by either creditors or owners.

visual_beats.directive: Non-current assets block settles on the pan
Three current asset tiles stack beside it
Current asset counter reaches fifty thousand
Total assets label locks at two hundred thirty thousand

scenes.voiceover_script: Load the left pan. Non-current assets are property, machinery and other assets not turned into cash within one year: grooming tables, dryers and the shop leasehold, worth one hundred eighty thousand dollars. Current assets become cash within one year: twenty-four thousand of inventory, sixteen thousand of trade receivables and ten thousand of cash. That is fifty thousand dollars of current assets. Total assets are one hundred eighty thousand plus fifty thousand, or two hundred thirty thousand dollars.

elements.label: Gap of $120,000: equity still to be added

visual_beats.directive: Payables tile lands on the right pan
Overdraft tile adds ten thousand
Long-term loan block settles in
Right pan holds $110,000 against $230,000 on the left; equity of $120,000 is still missing

scenes.voiceover_script: Fill the right pan. Current liabilities are short-term debts due within one year: thirty thousand dollars owed to suppliers and a ten-thousand-dollar overdraft, totalling forty thousand. Non-current liabilities are long-term debts repaid over more than one year: a seventy-thousand-dollar bank loan for equipment. Total liabilities are forty thousand plus seventy thousand, or one hundred ten thousand dollars. The right pan is still far lighter than the left, so the owners' equity is needed to balance the scale.

visual_beats.directive: Equity tile rises into the right pan
Three right-hand figures add together
Beam swings gently to horizontal
Equality label flashes on both pans

scenes.voiceover_script: Equity completes the right pan. The owners invested one hundred twenty thousand dollars. Add current liabilities of forty thousand, non-current liabilities of seventy thousand, and equity of one hundred twenty thousand. Forty plus seventy plus one hundred twenty equals two hundred thirty thousand dollars. The scale levels perfectly: total assets of two hundred thirty thousand equal total liabilities plus equity. If the two sides did not agree, a figure would be missing.

on_screen_labels: Method: total assets minus current liabilities

visual_beats.directive: First card subtracts current liabilities
Second card defines capital employed
Check card repeats the result
Both answers lock together

scenes.voiceover_script: Two derived figures matter. Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities: fifty thousand minus forty thousand equals ten thousand dollars. Capital employed, defined here as total assets minus current liabilities, is two hundred thirty thousand minus forty thousand, or one hundred ninety thousand dollars. Check it the other way: non-current assets of one hundred eighty thousand plus working capital of ten thousand also gives one hundred ninety thousand.

visual_beats.directive: Current Ratio card builds first
Inventory bucket, 48% of current assets, lifts out
Acid-Test Ratio 0.65 appears weaker than Current Ratio 1.25
Judgement beam tips toward caution over stock dependence

scenes.voiceover_script: Assess liquidity. The Current Ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities: fifty thousand over forty thousand gives one point two five to one. The Acid-Test Ratio removes inventory: fifty thousand minus twenty-four thousand is twenty-six thousand, divided by forty thousand gives zero point six five to one. Because nearly half of current assets, forty-eight percent, are shampoos and brushes in stock, therefore the firm depends on selling inventory, so its liquid cover is weaker than the first ratio suggests.

on_screen_labels: Historic cost and one date only

visual_beats.directive: Left panel lists lender and owner uses
Historic cost tag appears on assets
Goodwill and skill tiles stay empty
Income Statement sits beside the snapshot

scenes.voiceover_script: A statement of financial position is useful to lenders and owners, because it shows what is owed and what is owned. But it is a snapshot: figures are at historical cost, not today's market value; goodwill and staff skill are absent; and one date can hide a seasonal cash gap. A single list of balances cannot show profit earned during the year. Read it alongside the Income Statement before lending or investing.

elements.label: Scale level at two hundred thirty thousand

visual_beats.directive: Left pan totals two hundred thirty thousand
Right pan matches it exactly
Ratio cards slide out on either side
Quiz prompt fades in over the beam

scenes.voiceover_script: Rebalance the scale one last time. Left pan: non-current assets one hundred eighty thousand, current assets fifty thousand, total two hundred thirty thousand. Right pan: current liabilities forty thousand, non-current liabilities seventy thousand, equity one hundred twenty thousand, total two hundred thirty thousand. Working capital ten thousand; capital employed one hundred ninety thousand. Current Ratio one point two five; Acid-Test Ratio zero point six five. The picture is clear at a glance, yet only for this one date.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Paw & Polish has $50,000 current assets including $24,000 inventory, and $40,000 current liabilities. Which liquidity conclusion is correct?
options: Current Ratio 1.25:1 and Acid-Test Ratio 0.65:1, so it relies on selling inventory
Liquidity is strong because inventory is cash
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: Two ratio cards appear; the inventory bucket is lifted out of the current-assets bar and the second card drops below 1, while the first card stays above 1.

videos.video_title: Five Ratios, One Dataset
learning_objectives: Calculate Current Ratio and Acid-Test Ratio to two decimal places
Calculate Gross Profit Margin, Profit Margin and ROCE to two decimal places
Interpret liquidity and profitability side by side and state limitations

visual_beats.directive: Income Statement card reveals five figures
Financial position card reveals four figures
Capital employed card locks at two hundred forty thousand
Liquidity and profitability labels split apart

scenes.voiceover_script: Meet Inkwell Notebook Press, which publishes pocket notebooks. One dataset drives five ratios. From its Income Statement: revenue two hundred thousand dollars, cost of sales one hundred twenty thousand, gross profit eighty thousand, expenses fifty thousand, profit thirty thousand. From its statement of financial position: current assets ninety thousand, inventory eighteen thousand, current liabilities sixty thousand, and capital employed two hundred forty thousand. Liquidity tests short-term survival; profitability tests earning power.

elements.label: Current assets divided by current liabilities
One dollar fifty per dollar owed

visual_beats.directive: Formula card slides in from the left
Ninety thousand and sixty thousand glow
Division sign flashes
Answer card reads one point five zero to one

scenes.voiceover_script: First ratio: the Current Ratio measures liquidity. Formula: current assets divided by current liabilities. Substitute ninety thousand dollars over sixty thousand dollars. Ninety divided by sixty equals one point five. The Current Ratio is one point five zero to one. Inkwell holds one dollar fifty of current assets for every dollar of short-term debt. That looks comfortable, but current assets include inventory that may not sell quickly.

elements.label: Current assets minus inventory over current liabilities

visual_beats.directive: Formula card appears with brackets
Inventory tile lifts out of the asset bar
Numerator changes to seventy-two thousand
Answer card reads one point two zero to one

scenes.voiceover_script: Second ratio: the Acid-Test Ratio is current assets minus inventories, divided by current liabilities. Substitute ninety thousand minus eighteen thousand, giving seventy-two thousand, over sixty thousand. Seventy-two divided by sixty equals one point two; the Acid-Test Ratio is one point two zero to one. This strips out stock, so it is a harsher liquidity test. Inkwell still covers each dollar of short-term debt with one dollar twenty of liquid assets.

elements.label: Forty percent green segment of sales

visual_beats.directive: Formula card shows times one hundred
Two figures glow in the fraction
Wheel fills forty percent green
Answer card locks at forty point zero zero percent

scenes.voiceover_script: Third ratio: Gross Profit Margin measures profitability. Formula: gross profit divided by revenue, times one hundred. Substitute eighty thousand over two hundred thousand, times one hundred. Eighty divided by two hundred is zero point four; the Gross Profit Margin is forty point zero zero percent. That means forty cents of every sales dollar remains after direct costs, before overheads. Compare it with the profit margin to see what overheads take.

elements.label: Forty percent bar versus fifteen percent bar

visual_beats.directive: Formula card slides into the left panel
Overhead segment eats twenty-five points
Net bar settles at fifteen percent
Answer card reads fifteen point zero zero percent

scenes.voiceover_script: Fourth ratio: Profit Margin. Formula: profit divided by revenue, times one hundred. Substitute thirty thousand over two hundred thousand, times one hundred. Thirty divided by two hundred is zero point one five; Profit Margin is fifteen point zero zero percent. Gross Profit Margin was forty percent, so overheads consumed twenty-five percentage points of sales. Because expenses are large, therefore net profit is thin, so rising rent would hurt quickly.

elements.label: Return dial turns to twelve point five

visual_beats.directive: Capital employed card shows two hundred forty thousand
Profit figure glows in numerator
Dial sweeps around to twelve point five
Answer card locks at twelve point five zero percent

scenes.voiceover_script: Fifth ratio: ROCE, return on capital employed. Formula: profit divided by capital employed, times one hundred. Capital employed is two hundred forty thousand dollars. Substitute thirty thousand over two hundred forty thousand, times one hundred. Thirty divided by two hundred forty is one eighth; ROCE is twelve point five zero percent. Every hundred dollars invested in the press earns twelve dollars fifty of profit each year.

visual_beats.directive: Three liquidity gauges settle
Three profitability bars rise side by side
Lender icon nods at liquid cover
Owner icon weighs the moderate return

scenes.voiceover_script: Place liquidity and profitability side by side. Current Ratio one point five zero, Acid-Test Ratio one point two zero: short-term cover looks sound. Gross Profit Margin forty percent, Profit Margin fifteen percent, ROCE twelve point five zero percent: the press earns steadily but not spectacularly. Because inventory is modest relative to current assets, therefore liquid cover is credible, so a lender may feel safe while an owner seeks higher returns.

visual_beats.directive: Left panel turns numbers into signals
Historic cost stamp appears on the right
Qualitative tiles fade in but stay unmeasured
Multi-year grid overlays the scene

scenes.voiceover_script: Now the limits. Ratios use historic figures and one year's snapshot; different firms use different accounting policies. They ignore non-financial factors like customer loyalty, staff skill and product quality. A good ratio cannot prove future returns. Yet ratios still turn a pile of numbers into comparable signals: liquidity for survival, profitability for efficiency. Use several years and several competitors before deciding on Inkwell.

visual_beats.directive: Five result cards line up
Liquidity pair glows green
Profitability trio glows blue
Quiz prompt appears over the balanced cards

scenes.voiceover_script: Time for a recap. Five formulas, one dataset. Liquidity: Current Ratio and Acid-Test Ratio. Profitability: Gross Profit Margin, Profit Margin and ROCE. Results: one point five zero, one point two zero, forty percent, fifteen percent and twelve point five zero percent. The question on screen asks you to interpret, not just recite. Choose the conclusion that both the profit and the liquid asset figures support.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Inkwell's Profit Margin is 15.00% and its Acid-Test Ratio is 1.20:1. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: It earns profit on sales and has $1.20 of liquid assets per $1 of short-term debt
It holds no inventory at all
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: A profit bar marked 15.00% and a liquid-asset stack marked 1.20:1 slide together into one judgement card, while the no-inventory and cannot-cover tiles fade away.

videos.unit_title: Unit 6: External influences on business activity
videos.video_title: Visualising the Business Cycle and Policy Levers
learning_objectives: Describe the four stages of the business cycle and their effects on demand, output and employment
Explain how inflation, unemployment and GDP influence business decisions
Evaluate fiscal and monetary policy using a concrete bicycle factory scenario

visual_beats.directive: Fade in empty ring
Arrows begin to orbit
Four stage gates light up

scenes.voiceover_script: Meet Brambledon Bicycles, a mid sized maker of city bikes. A glowing loop turns through growth, boom, recession and slump. Arrows advance around the ring. Watch arrows pass four gates, one for each stage. Each stage shifts demand, output, employment and the goals this firm can pursue.

visual_beats.directive: Unroll the ring into a line
Demand curve rises then falls
Workforce tiles add and shrink
Loop arrow returns to growth

scenes.voiceover_script: During growth, orders rise and Brambledon adds shifts. In the boom, demand is strong but wages climb as workers become scarce. Recession brings falling orders and spare capacity. Slump means deep cuts, job losses and a fight for cash. Notice how demand, output and employment all move together around the loop every time. The arrow then returns to growth, so the pattern repeats again and again.

visual_beats.directive: Index tile climbs from 100
Price tiles grow
Workforce tiles thin out
Purchasing power bar shrinks

scenes.voiceover_script: Inflation means the average price level of goods and services rises over time. An index tile climbs from one hundred to one hundred five, so a hundred dollars buys less. Employment supports demand, but tight labour pushes wages up. Unemployment means willing workers cannot find jobs, weakening demand for bikes. Higher material costs squeeze margin unless Brambledon raises prices, which may cost sales in a competitive market.

visual_beats.directive: Gauge dial appears
Quarter bars turn red
Second negative quarter lights

scenes.voiceover_script: Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the total value of output of goods and services in a country in one year. Economic growth is when real GDP increases. A recession is falling GDP, usually two consecutive quarters of negative growth. Brambledon watches these figures before planning stock. If GDP falls for two quarters, the firm delays its new frame line.

visual_beats.directive: Console levers slide in
Corporation tax lever lifts
Pipes feed outcome tiles
Demand tile responds

scenes.voiceover_script: Fiscal policy uses taxation and public spending to influence demand. Corporation tax comes out of retained profit, leaving less for Brambledon to invest. Higher income tax cuts disposable income, so customers buy fewer bikes. More government spending can create orders, or compete for scarce resources and push costs up. A lower tax rate leaves more cash, but the government then collects less to spend on services.

visual_beats.directive: Rate lever moves from 3 to 7
Loan cost pipe glows
Workshop icon dims
Spending bar contracts

scenes.voiceover_script: Monetary policy works through interest rates. Brambledon's loan rate rises from three percent to seven percent. Because borrowing costs rise, monthly repayments take more profit, so the firm postpones a new workshop. Customers face dearer credit too, and consumer spending falls. Lower rates would reverse both effects. The transmission runs from the rate, to the loan, to spending, then to orders and to jobs across the supply chain.

on_screen_labels: CON: rate rises make loans dear

visual_beats.directive: Green pro panel fills
Red con panel fills
Rate lever moves both ways
Balance icon settles

scenes.voiceover_script: On one side, lower rates and lower taxes lift demand and profit. Brambledon can hire and expand. On the other side, cheap credit can fuel inflation, and rate rises make loans expensive. Higher taxes reduce profit but fund services that support demand. Which lever matters most depends on whether the problem is weak sales or rising costs. A boom needs cooling, while a slump needs stimulus, so policy must match the stage of the cycle we are in.

visual_beats.directive: Cost valve closes
Expansion line dims
Product mix funnel shifts
Training tile stays lit

scenes.voiceover_script: During a downturn Brambledon acts. Because orders fall and cash is tight, therefore it cuts overtime and delays expansion, so it protects cash. It changes product mix toward cheaper commuter bikes, negotiates supplier terms and targets students. Cutting costs preserves the firm, but deep cuts can damage quality and morale. A firm that keeps training may recover faster when growth returns. Stock is reduced, prices are held where possible, and new models are postponed until demand improves. The lesson is to match spending to the stage of the cycle.

scenes.on_screen_title: Apply It: Two Levers, One Firm

visual_beats.directive: Both levers appear
Rate lever rises
Tax lever falls
Arrows reveal the answer

scenes.voiceover_script: Time to apply this. Imagine interest rates rise and income tax falls at the same time. Which effect hits Brambledon first, and which is more significant for a firm with a large loan? On screen, two levers move in opposite directions. Choose your answer, then watch the arrows show the result. A larger loan means heavier repayments, so the rate rise usually bites harder than extra spending power from tax in the short run for this business.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Brambledon has a large loan. Interest rates rise from 3% to 7% while income tax falls. Which effect is most significant first?
options: Dearer loan repayments reduce profit and delay investment
Lower income tax instantly doubles bicycle sales
Higher rates make borrowing cheaper for the firm
Falling income tax removes the need to repay loans
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: The rate lever slides from 3 to 7 and a red repayment pipe widens into the profit tile, while the green tax lever only nudges the spending bar. The loan arrow reaches the workshop before the customer arrow reaches the showroom.

videos.unit_title: Unit 6: External influences on business activity
videos.video_title: Visualising Externalities, Ethics and Pressure Groups
learning_objectives: Distinguish private and social costs and benefits using spillover animations
Explain sustainable development as a balance of economic, social and environmental pillars
Evaluate ethical objectives against profit objectives with a cocoa factory scenario

visual_beats.directive: Factory appears
Red and amber arrows spill out
Green benefit arrow appears

scenes.voiceover_script: Meet Cocoa Grove Collective, a co operative that runs a cocoa processing plant. Thick arrows spill out of the factory: smoke, waste water and jobs. Some spillovers harm neighbours, others help them. These effects sit outside the firm's own accounts, yet they shape real decisions for everyone nearby.

visual_beats.directive: Private stack builds to 150000
External stack builds to 400000
Spillover arrow crosses
Total tile reads 550000

scenes.voiceover_script: External costs are costs imposed on a third party, independent of the original transaction. The plant pays one hundred fifty thousand dollars to treat waste water. Untreated discharge would impose four hundred thousand dollars of cleanup and health costs on the town. Social cost is private cost plus external cost: five hundred fifty thousand dollars. The price of cocoa does not include that damage, so the market overproduces it.

visual_beats.directive: Private benefit builds to 120000
External benefit builds to 200000
Trainee tiles appear

scenes.voiceover_script: External benefits are gains imposed on a third party, independent of the transaction. A training scheme gives Cocoa Grove one hundred twenty thousand dollars of extra productivity. It also gives the community two hundred thousand dollars of skills. Social benefit is private plus external, three hundred twenty thousand dollars. The firm gains too, because trained workers make fewer mistakes.

visual_beats.directive: Three pillars rise
Platform balances on top
Environmental pillar shrinks
Platform tilts then recovers

scenes.voiceover_script: Sustainable development means meeting today's needs without damaging tomorrow's. On screen, three pillars hold up a platform: economic profit, social fairness and environmental care. If one pillar shrinks, the platform tilts. Cocoa Grove must earn enough, pay fairly and protect the river, or the whole business becomes unstable. A fair price to farmers keeps the supply chain reliable. Clean water keeps the licence. Both protect long term profit.

visual_beats.directive: Wage meter rises from 8
Worker tiles multiply across 50 weeks
Cocoa sack price rises
Two cost totals appear

scenes.voiceover_script: Ethical issues create conflicts. Wages here are eight dollars an hour; a fair wage is ten. For one hundred twenty workers on forty hour weeks across fifty working weeks, that adds four hundred eighty thousand dollars a year. Certified cocoa costs two thousand one hundred dollars a tonne instead of one thousand eight hundred, adding six hundred thousand dollars on two thousand tonnes. Cheaper inputs lift short term margin, but they may hide child labour and damage the co operative's reputation.

visual_beats.directive: Crowd icon appears
Waves ripple toward firm
Sales bar loses 8 percent
Shield rises

scenes.voiceover_script: A pressure group is people acting together to force businesses or governments to adopt policies. Campaign waves roll over Cocoa Grove on screen. Twelve thousand subscribers share a boycott call. If eight percent of five million dollars of sales is lost, that is four hundred thousand dollars. Firms can engage, publish transparent reports or change suppliers. Ignoring legitimate concerns can escalate reputational damage and invite legal action.

on_screen_labels: CON: higher costs and price gap
CON: fair wages may cut jobs

visual_beats.directive: Green ethics panel fills
Red profit panel fills
Price tag slides upward
Balance icon judges

scenes.voiceover_script: Two sides, one decision. Being ethical can improve reputation, attract customers and employees, and reduce legal risk. Loyal buyers may accept a higher price. Yet ethical sourcing raises costs, and a price disadvantage can lose price sensitive orders. Paying fair wages may force job cuts instead of fairer jobs. The balance depends on whether customers value the story enough to pay. In a downturn, cost cutting may win the argument; in a boom, brand trust can win it for this co operative and its buyers.

scenes.on_screen_title: Cocoa Grove Chooses a Middle Path

visual_beats.directive: Treatment pipe starts
Premium lane lights green
Standard lane lights amber
River tile turns blue

scenes.voiceover_script: Cocoa Grove chooses a middle path. Because untreated waste harms the river, therefore the firm installs treatment and raises prices slightly, so the licence is safe. It keeps certified cocoa for its premium line and cheaper beans for standard bars. That protects margin and reputation at once. Transparent reporting turns the pressure group from an opponent into a critic it can answer. Costs rise, but sales hold and the town keeps its clean water supply for years.

scenes.on_screen_title: Apply It: Cheap Beans or Certified Beans

visual_beats.directive: Fork appears
Cheap path flashes red
Certified path flashes green
Both outcome tiles settle

scenes.voiceover_script: Apply the idea. Cocoa Grove can buy cheap beans from a supplier that pollutes, or certified beans that cost three hundred dollars more per tonne. Which choice protects profit and which protects the brand? On screen, two paths split into cost and reputation tiles. Pick one, then see the downstream effects. A boycott could erase four hundred thousand dollars of sales, while the premium line keeps loyal buyers.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: Cocoa Grove can save $600,000 by using a polluting supplier. A boycott may erase $400,000 of sales. What is the best justification for staying certified?
options: Reputation and licence protection can outweigh the short term saving
Certified cocoa always lowers the immediate material bill
Pressure groups have no influence on consumer behaviour
External costs are always paid by the supplier alone
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: Two supplier paths split. The cheap path shows a green $600,000 saving tile then a red $400,000 boycott wave, while the certified path keeps the premium lane and clean river tile lit. The balance icon tips toward the certified path.

videos.unit_title: Unit 6: External influences on business activity
videos.video_title: Visualising Globalisation, Exchange Rates and Trade Gates
learning_objectives: Describe globalisation and the parent to subsidiary flows of a multinational
Calculate and interpret exchange rate conversions and direction of price changes
Evaluate tariffs and quotas against free trade using numeric border gate examples

visual_beats.directive: Globe fades in
Nodes connect with lines
Trade flows animate

scenes.voiceover_script: Meet Northstar Microchip Imports, a British firm buying sensors from abroad. A glowing network links markets. Lines thicken as containers and data cross borders. This is globalisation: worldwide trade and the movement of people and capital between countries. Northstar sits on one small node, but the whole web moves it.

visual_beats.directive: Transport links brighten
Buyer nodes light up green
Rival nodes flash red
Assembly line pauses

scenes.voiceover_script: Globalisation opens markets. Improved transport, faster communication and free trade agreements let Northstar reach buyers in six countries. Brand awareness spreads online. But threats travel with the same links: overseas rivals undercut prices, and a shock in one country travels along every line. The network creates opportunity and vulnerability together. A supplier strike overseas can stop the assembly line here, so managers watch the whole map.

visual_beats.directive: Parent node appears
Capital arrow descends
Subsidiary adds 150 jobs
Profit arrow ascends
