scenes.voiceover_script: Now watch Vantara Devices, a multinational with operations in more than one country. Its parent sends two million dollars of capital to Vantara Assembly Works. The subsidiary creates one hundred fifty jobs and earns five million dollars of exports. Six hundred thousand dollars of profit flows back to the parent. Host countries gain investment, jobs and choice, but face competition and profit repatriation and pressure on local firms.

visual_beats.directive: Rate card slides in
400 dollar card enters
Multiply by 0.75 shows 300
Cards flip to show reverse

scenes.voiceover_script: Exchange rates state one currency in terms of another. Here one dollar buys seventy five pence. A British buyer paying four hundred dollars for sensors needs three hundred pounds, because four hundred times nought point seven five equals three hundred. Reverse it: a three hundred pound order costs an American buyer four hundred dollars. Cards animate both directions. Every purchase crosses the rate, so every price changes twice.

visual_beats.directive: Rate card flips to 0.60
Divide 300 by 0.60 shows 500
Export arrow rises
Import arrow falls to 240

scenes.voiceover_script: Now the dollar depreciates: one dollar buys sixty pence, so the pound appreciates. The same three hundred pound order now costs the American buyer five hundred dollars, because three hundred divided by nought point six is five hundred. British exports are dearer. Meanwhile a four hundred dollar American order costs a British buyer two hundred forty pounds, not three hundred, so imports are cheaper. Northstar gains on costs, but its sales slow.

scenes.on_screen_title: Tariff: The Border Gate Adds a Tax
on_screen_labels: Tariff is a tax on imports

visual_beats.directive: 400 dollar component reaches gate
Ten percent stamp lands
Funnel adds 40 dollars
Cost tile reads 330 pounds

scenes.voiceover_script: A tariff is a tax put on imported goods entering the country. Here a border gate adds a ten percent tariff to a four hundred dollar component. That is forty dollars, so the landed cost becomes four hundred forty dollars. At one dollar to seventy five pence, Northstar pays three hundred thirty pounds instead of three hundred. The gate closes on cheap inputs and opens for local rivals.

scenes.on_screen_title: Quota: The Border Gate Limits Quantity

visual_beats.directive: Twelve thousand units queue
Gate closes at eight thousand
Four thousand gap appears
Price tile reaches 330

scenes.voiceover_script: A quota is a limit on the physical quantity of a product that can be imported. At the border gate, twelve thousand sensors are wanted but only eight thousand pass. The four thousand unit gap pushes the price up from three hundred to three hundred thirty pounds. Domestic producers sell more, while Northstar faces higher costs and less choice. It may switch to local suppliers, or pass the increase to customers.

visual_beats.directive: Open network glows green
Gate pair slams red
Cost and job tiles compare
Balance icon settles

scenes.voiceover_script: Free trade and protection each have two sides. Free trade gives Northstar cheaper inputs, wider markets and more choice. Because competition is strong, therefore prices fall, so consumers benefit. Yet domestic firms can be squeezed and jobs lost. Protection saves jobs and infant industries, but tariffs raise costs, quotas limit supply and other countries may retaliate. For an importing firm, the balance tilts toward free trade. If the pound appreciates, imports get cheaper anyway, so a tariff hurts less. If the dollar strengthens, protection may look kinder.

visual_beats.directive: Two rate cards appear
Second card flips to 0.60
Bill tile changes to 240
Price arrows settle

scenes.voiceover_script: Now apply it. One dollar buys seventy five pence. A British firm owes four hundred dollars to a supplier. Later the dollar depreciates to sixty pence. What does the bill become in pounds, and are its exports dearer or cheaper for American buyers? On screen, two currency cards flip and a border gate opens. Choose, then watch the arrows settle. Two hundred forty pounds is the new bill, so imports are cheaper. A three hundred pound export now costs five hundred dollars, so overseas buyers pay more.

end_of_video_recap_quiz.question: At $1 = 0.75 pounds a British importing firm owes $400. If the dollar depreciates to $1 = 0.60 pounds, what happens to the bill in pounds and to British exports sold to America?
options: The bill falls to 240 pounds and exports become dearer in dollars
The bill rises to 500 pounds and exports become cheaper in dollars
The bill stays at 400 pounds because rates do not affect trade
The bill falls to 240 pounds and exports become cheaper in dollars
end_of_video_recap_quiz.visual_explanation: The rate card flips from 0.75 to 0.60, the 400 dollar bill tile shrinks from 300 to 240 pounds, and the export arrow rises from 400 to 500 dollars while the import arrow falls.
